question: Some fashion brands are now using AI-generated models instead of human ones in campaigns. What do you think about that trend, and would you have reservations working on a campaign that used one?
lookingFor: Reasoned engagement with a live industry debate that weighs cost and creative benefits against labour and representation concerns, without a knee-jerk verdict.

bullets: Acknowledge the genuine commercial appeal: cost, speed, infinite variation, no shoot logistics
Weigh it against real costs: fewer paid jobs for models, questions about authenticity and representation
Land on a personal, non-evasive position, ideally with a condition under which they'd be comfortable
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I understand why brands are drawn to it, an AI model never gets tired, can be resized instantly for every market, and skips the cost of a full shoot, which matters a lot for a smaller label. But it worries me too, because it quietly removes paid work from real models and stylists, and it can present a body that isn't real as if it were, which feels like a step backward after years of brands being pushed toward honest representation. I'd personally be comfortable working on it if the brand was transparent that the image was AI-generated, but I'd push back hard on using it to quietly replace diverse casting rather than expand what's creatively possible. I don't think the technology is the problem, I think it's whether brands use it honestly.

commonMistakes: Dismissing AI models outright with no acknowledgment of the commercial logic
Enthusiastically endorsing it with no mention of labour or authenticity concerns
Refusing to state a personal position
followUps: Would your answer change if the AI model was styled to look like a specific real influencer without their consent?

question: Platforms like Vinted and Depop have made resale mainstream. Is that a threat to a fashion brand's marketing, or an opportunity?
lookingFor: Structured reasoning about how resale affects both brand exposure and new-item sales, rather than treating it as purely good or bad.

bullets: Note the threat: resale can cannibalise full-price sales and dilute exclusivity for some brands
Note the opportunity: resale extends brand reach to new, often younger, budget-conscious buyers and signals durability
Mention brand-run resale or trade-in schemes as a way to capture the value instead of losing it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It's genuinely both. For a brand that competes on exclusivity, seeing pieces resold cheaply can undercut the story they're trying to tell about scarcity. But for most brands I think it's actually an opportunity, because it puts the label in front of buyers who couldn't afford it new and often converts them into full-price customers later, and it quietly signals the clothes are well made enough to be worth reselling. What I find smart is when brands run their own resale or trade-in programme instead of leaving that value entirely to a third-party platform, because then they keep the customer relationship and the data instead of handing it to Vinted. I'd want to work somewhere treating resale as a channel to design for, not a threat to ignore.

commonMistakes: Treating resale as purely a threat with no upside considered
Ignoring how resale affects different brand tiers differently
Not mentioning brand-owned resale as a strategic response
followUps: Which type of brand do you think has the most to lose from resale, and why?

question: Do you know what a retail media network is, and why fashion brands are spending more of their advertising budget there?
lookingFor: Genuine grasp of a fast-growing, less consumer-visible corner of the industry, showing research beyond obvious consumer-facing marketing.

bullets: Define retail media as advertising space sold by a retailer on its own site, app, or in-store screens, using its own purchase data
Explain why it's attractive: highly targeted, tied directly to a purchase moment, and measurable
Note the trade-off: brands become dependent on the retailer's platform and data rather than owning it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A retail media network is when a retailer, like an Amazon or a Zalando, sells ad space on its own site or app using the purchase data it already holds, so a brand can put a product in front of someone who's already shown buying intent for that category. It's grown fast because it's some of the most accountable advertising a brand can buy, you can see the ad and the sale in the same platform, unlike a lot of social advertising where the link to a purchase is fuzzier. The trade-off that interests me is that it makes brands more dependent on the retailer's data and audience rather than building their own, which is a bit of a step back from the direct-to-consumer push of the last decade. I think the smart brands are treating it as one channel among several rather than betting everything on it.

commonMistakes: Confusing retail media with basic social media advertising
No mention of the data or targeting advantage that makes it valuable
Missing the dependency trade-off entirely
followUps: How would you decide how much budget to shift from social ads into retail media?

question: Live shopping and in-app checkout, like TikTok Shop, have taken off in a way they never quite did in the West a few years ago. Why do you think it's working now?
lookingFor: Awareness of a current shift in how fashion is sold, with reasoning about why the timing and mechanics finally made it work.

bullets: Note the mechanism: removing friction by letting people buy without leaving the app or the video
Mention trust drivers: creator recommendation and real-time demonstration reducing purchase hesitation
Connect it to a broader shift toward entertainment-driven, impulse-friendly shopping
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think it's mostly about friction. Every extra tap between seeing something and buying it loses people, and in-app checkout collapses that entire journey into one screen, which earlier attempts at social shopping never quite managed. It also works because it borrows trust from a creator showing the product live, trying it on, answering comments in real time, which feels far more convincing than a static product photo. I think it's really shopping dressed up as entertainment, and once platforms made the actual transaction seamless, that combination finally had somewhere to land. I'd be curious how brands keep the return rates manageable, since impulse-driven buying usually comes with higher returns.

commonMistakes: Describing it as just 'social media is popular' with no mechanism
Ignoring the friction-removal aspect of in-app checkout
No acknowledgment of any downside like returns or impulse buying
followUps: What kind of fashion product do you think is best suited to live shopping, and what kind isn't?

question: Imagine you're asked to run a campaign encouraging customers to buy a new 'micro-trend' capsule every few weeks, the kind of thing that drives haul culture online. Would you take the brief?
lookingFor: Honest ethical reasoning about a marketer's role in driving overconsumption, without either refusing to engage or accepting uncritically.

bullets: Acknowledge the tension directly: this is the job, but it has a real environmental and behavioural cost
Reason through whether and how they'd take the brief rather than giving a flat yes or no
Land on a considered position, possibly proposing how they'd shape the brief differently
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I wouldn't refuse it outright, because driving purchase is genuinely the job, but I also wouldn't take it without pushing back a little on how it's framed. I'd want to understand who the capsule is aimed at and whether the pace is realistic for people to actually wear the pieces rather than discard them after one video, because that's really where the harm sits. If I could, I'd try to shift the brief toward fewer, better pieces marketed with more intensity rather than more items marketed more often, since that still hits a sales target without leaning quite so hard into disposability. I don't think I'd walk away from the job over it, but I'd want to be someone who nudges the brief rather than just executing it as handed to me.

commonMistakes: Refusing the brief entirely with no engagement with the commercial reality
Accepting it with no ethical reflection at all
Vague hand-wringing with no actual position or proposed action
followUps: What would you say if your manager told you the pushback wasn't your place?

question: Regulators in the EU and elsewhere have started cracking down on vague sustainability claims like 'eco-friendly' and 'conscious'. What impact do you think that will have on how fashion brands market themselves?
lookingFor: Awareness of a real, current regulatory shift and its practical consequences for marketing language and claims.

bullets: Show awareness that regulators now require substantiated, specific claims rather than vague eco-language
Explain the practical impact: brands need verifiable data, certifications, or third-party standards behind any claim
Note this could actually help honest brands stand out once vague greenwashing is harder to use
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: From what I've read, the direction is toward requiring claims to be specific and provable, so a label can't just print 'eco-friendly' on a tag without evidence, it needs to say something like the percentage of recycled material or point to a real certification. Practically that means marketing and sustainability teams have to work much more closely together, because copywriters can't invent language that the supply chain data doesn't actually support. I think it's a genuinely good shift, because it raises the cost of vague greenwashing and should make brands that are actually doing the work stand out more clearly instead of being drowned out by empty claims. It probably makes marketing sustainability harder to write, but more trustworthy when it lands.

commonMistakes: No awareness that such regulation exists or is developing
Treating it as purely a compliance burden with no upside
Vague answer with no mention of what specifically needs to change in claims
followUps: How would you rewrite a vague claim like 'made with love for the planet' to meet that bar?

question: A celebrity brand ambassador your team signed six months ago is now at the centre of a serious public scandal, right before your biggest campaign of the year launches featuring them. What would you want the team to consider?
lookingFor: Structured crisis thinking that weighs speed, evidence, and reputational risk rather than an instant reflexive call.

bullets: Avoid an instant reflexive decision; note the need to quickly assess the severity and credibility of the allegations
Weigh options beyond a binary: pause the campaign, delay, quietly reduce their presence, or fully sever ties
Consider the audience and long-term brand reputation, not just short-term media pressure
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My first instinct wouldn't be to panic and pull everything immediately, because acting on incomplete information can be its own mistake, but I also wouldn't sit on it while a launch date approaches. I'd want the team to quickly assess how serious and credible the situation is, since a minor controversy and a serious allegation call for very different responses. Depending on that, the options aren't just 'keep them' or 'cut them', there's also pausing the launch briefly, reducing their visual presence in the campaign, or issuing a clear statement while the facts settle. What I'd care most about is that whatever we decide isn't driven purely by short-term media pressure but by what actually protects the people the campaign might affect and the brand's credibility months from now.

commonMistakes: Jumping straight to 'drop them immediately' with no assessment of severity
Ignoring the option of anything other than a full keep-or-cut decision
Focusing only on short-term press reaction with no longer-term reasoning
followUps: How would your answer change if the allegations turned out to be false a week later?

question: With third-party cookies disappearing, how should a fashion brand go about building its own first-party data instead?
lookingFor: Concrete understanding of first-party data collection methods and the value exchange needed to get customers to share information willingly.

bullets: Give concrete mechanisms: loyalty programmes, email sign-ups, style quizzes, account creation at checkout
Emphasise the need for a genuine value exchange, not just asking for data
Note that first-party data is smaller in scale but far more reliable and permission-based than third-party tracking
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The brands doing it well don't just ask for an email address, they give people a reason to hand it over, like a style quiz that gives useful recommendations back, or a loyalty programme with real perks like early access to drops. Account creation at checkout and post-purchase surveys are quieter ways to build the same picture over time. What I think matters most is that it's a genuine value exchange rather than a data grab, because people will notice if they're giving information and getting nothing meaningful back, and that erodes trust fast. It's a smaller pool of data than third-party tracking gave brands, but it's more accurate and it's data people actually agreed to share, which feels like the right trade to be making.

commonMistakes: Vague statements about 'collecting more data' with no concrete method
Ignoring the need for a value exchange to earn the data
Confusing first-party data with buying third-party data lists
followUps: What would you offer a customer in exchange for their birthday and sizing information?

question: Acquiring a new customer is far more expensive than keeping an existing one. How would you design a loyalty programme for a mid-range fashion brand?
lookingFor: Reasoning about retention economics and a loyalty design that goes beyond a generic points system.

bullets: Show understanding of why retention matters more than pure acquisition cost
Move beyond simple points-per-pound toward experiential or status-based rewards, like early access or events
Note the need to track whether the programme actually changes repeat purchase behaviour, not just enrolment
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A basic points-per-pound scheme is easy to copy and rarely changes behaviour much, so I'd want something with a status element people actually feel, like tiers that unlock early access to new drops or invites to a small in-store event, because status and access tend to matter more than a small discount for fashion specifically. I'd also want the rewards to feel personal, using purchase history to surprise someone with something relevant rather than a generic voucher. The part I'd insist on is measuring it properly, tracking whether members actually buy more often after joining rather than just counting sign-ups, because a loyalty programme that boosts enrolment numbers without changing repeat purchase behaviour isn't actually doing its job.

commonMistakes: Designing a generic points system with no differentiation
Not mentioning how success would actually be measured
Focusing entirely on discounts with no experiential or status element
followUps: What would make you cancel or redesign a loyalty programme after a year?

question: Why would a fashion brand invest in a temporary pop-up store when it could put that budget into digital advertising instead?
lookingFor: Understanding of what physical, experiential retail achieves that digital advertising alone cannot, with awareness of its limits.

bullets: Explain what a pop-up achieves that digital ads don't: physical brand immersion, press coverage, and social content generation
Note it works particularly well for testing a new market or product line at lower risk than a permanent store
Acknowledge the limits: it's expensive per visitor and hard to scale or measure precisely
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A pop-up does something a digital ad can't, it lets someone physically stand inside the brand's world for a few minutes, which tends to generate a kind of emotional memory and its own social content that a banner ad rarely creates. It's also a genuinely useful way to test a new city or product line without committing to a permanent lease, so it works as market research as much as marketing. The trade-off is that it's expensive per person who actually walks through the door, and it's much harder to measure precisely than a digital campaign where you can track every click. I think it makes most sense as a complement to digital rather than a replacement, especially for a launch moment that needs a physical anchor.

commonMistakes: Treating pop-ups as purely nostalgic with no strategic rationale
Ignoring the cost-per-visitor and measurement limitations
Not mentioning its use as low-risk market testing
followUps: How would you measure whether a pop-up was actually worth the investment?

question: Counterfeit versions of popular fashion products are everywhere online, sometimes sold through the very platforms a brand advertises on. How should a marketing team think about that problem?
lookingFor: Awareness that counterfeiting is partly a marketing and platform-relationship issue, not just a legal one, with balanced reasoning.

bullets: Note the direct harm: lost revenue, damaged trust when a customer unknowingly buys a fake, and diluted brand value
Recognise it's not purely a legal team's problem; marketing can support through authentication tools, customer education, and platform pressure
Show awareness of the awkward tension when the counterfeit is sold on a platform the brand also advertises on
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It's easy to think of counterfeiting as purely a legal problem, but I think marketing has a real role too, because a customer who unknowingly buys a fake and gets a bad product still blames the brand, not the counterfeiter, and that quietly damages trust the brand spent years building. I'd want marketing involved in things like clear authentication tools, QR codes or verification pages that make it easy for a genuine buyer to check, and honest customer education about where to buy safely. The uncomfortable part is when the counterfeit is being sold through the exact platform the brand also advertises on, which puts marketing in the odd position of both funding and fighting the same channel, and I think that's a tension worth pushing the platform relationship team to actually address rather than ignoring.

commonMistakes: Treating counterfeiting as entirely a legal issue with no marketing role
No mention of the trust damage when a customer unknowingly buys a fake
Missing the awkward tension with platforms that host both ads and counterfeits
followUps: What would you say to a customer who bought a counterfeit believing it was genuine?

question: Limited hype drops deliberately create scarcity to drive demand, and a lot of the buyers chasing them are teenagers spending money they've saved up or borrowed. Is there an ethical line there for you?
lookingFor: Genuine ethical reasoning about a tactic the student may find exciting as a consumer, examined critically as a future practitioner.

bullets: Acknowledge scarcity marketing is a legitimate, effective, widely used tactic, not inherently wrong
Identify where it becomes ethically uncomfortable: deliberately targeting young or financially vulnerable buyers with urgency pressure
Propose where they'd personally draw a line rather than giving a purely abstract answer
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think scarcity itself is unethical, limited releases are a normal and honestly quite fun part of fashion culture, and plenty of adults chase them with money they can easily spare. Where it starts to bother me is when the targeting or the urgency tactics are clearly aimed at teenagers who might be spending money they've borrowed or saved for something else, because that's using a psychological trigger on people who are less equipped to resist it. My line would be around things like countdown timers and 'only 2 left' messaging stacked specifically on channels where the audience skews very young, especially if the product is priced well above what a typical teenager could reasonably afford. I'd be comfortable with scarcity as a tactic generally, just not comfortable turning up the pressure specifically on the people least able to handle it.

commonMistakes: Condemning all scarcity marketing as manipulative with no nuance
Dismissing the concern entirely because 'it's just marketing'
Giving an abstract answer with no personal line drawn
followUps: Would your view change if the product itself were something practical rather than a collectible sneaker?

question: A campaign concept your team has developed borrows heavily from a cultural tradition that isn't your own, and you're not sure the brand has done enough to credit or involve that culture properly. What would you do?
lookingFor: Careful ethical reasoning that distinguishes appreciation from appropriation and shows willingness to raise concerns constructively within a team.

bullets: Show understanding of the difference between respectful collaboration and extraction without credit or benefit
Describe a constructive way to raise the concern internally rather than staying silent or refusing to work at all
Suggest practical fixes: consulting people from that culture, crediting sources, involving them in the campaign itself
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd want to separate the idea itself, which might come from genuine admiration, from how it's actually being executed, because the difference between appreciation and appropriation is usually about whether the people the tradition belongs to are credited, consulted, or benefiting at all. I wouldn't stay quiet about it, but I also wouldn't just refuse to work on it, I'd raise it directly with whoever's leading the project and ask specifically what consultation had happened so far. If the answer was 'none', I'd push for bringing in people from that culture, whether as consultants, collaborators, or even the actual creative team, because that usually improves the work as well as making it more defensible. I think the goal is to make the campaign something that culture would recognise as respectful, not just something legal has cleared.

commonMistakes: Staying silent to avoid an awkward conversation
Refusing to work on it entirely without attempting to influence it constructively
Treating legal clearance as the same thing as cultural respect
followUps: What would you do if your manager dismissed the concern as overly sensitive?

question: More fashion brands are marketing collections as gender-neutral rather than splitting men's and women's lines. What do you think is driving that, and is it purely values-led or also commercial?
lookingFor: Balanced awareness of both the genuine cultural shift and the real commercial logic behind degendered collections.

bullets: Acknowledge the genuine cultural shift toward less rigid gender identity among younger consumers
Identify the commercial logic: a single range can be simpler to produce, market, and merchandise, widening the addressable audience
Note the risk of it being applied superficially just for a marketing narrative rather than a real design and buying shift
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think it's genuinely both. There's a real cultural shift, particularly among younger shoppers, toward not wanting clothing sorted so rigidly by gender in the first place, and brands that ignore that are out of step with a real part of their audience. But there's also a straightforward commercial logic, a single unified range can simplify design, production, and even store layout, and it widens who a piece is technically marketed to without needing two separate campaigns. What I'd want to check with any brand claiming to go gender-neutral is whether the actual product design and sizing reflect that, or whether it's really just a marketing label put on what's still effectively a men's cut. I think the ones doing it honestly are rethinking fit and sizing, not just the campaign language.

commonMistakes: Framing it as purely a values-driven decision with no commercial reasoning
Framing it as purely cynical marketing with no genuine cultural driver
Not questioning whether the shift is reflected in actual product, not just messaging
followUps: How would you market a gender-neutral collection differently from a traditional split-line launch?

question: What's the biggest marketing challenge in convincing someone to rent or subscribe to fashion instead of owning it?
lookingFor: Understanding of the psychological and practical barriers unique to rental fashion, and how marketing has to address them.

bullets: Identify the core barrier: attachment to ownership and hygiene or fit concerns about wearing something previously worn
Note that trust has to be built through logistics as much as messaging: cleaning standards, fit accuracy, easy returns
Show awareness of who the model actually suits: occasion wear or trend experimentation more than everyday basics
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think the biggest hurdle isn't really about price, it's the psychological shift away from ownership, plus a very practical worry about hygiene and fit when the item has been worn by strangers before. That means marketing rental can't just rely on nice messaging, it has to visibly build trust through the actual service, showing the cleaning process, making sizing information really reliable, and making returns effortless, because one bad experience will kill the whole idea for that customer. I also think it markets best for occasion wear or trying a trend before committing, rather than everyday basics people want to feel are fully theirs. Getting the positioning right for the right category seems like half the battle before any campaign even starts.

commonMistakes: Treating price as the only barrier to adoption
No mention of hygiene, fit, or trust as practical concerns
Ignoring which product categories actually suit the rental model
followUps: Which category of clothing do you think rental will never really work for, and why?

subtopic: Marketing to young or minor consumers
question: A fast-growing part of the market is tweens and young teenagers with their own spending power and social media accounts. How should a fashion marketer think about the responsibility of targeting that age group?
lookingFor: Careful reasoning about the extra duty of care owed to a young, impressionable audience without dismissing the commercial reality of the segment.

bullets: Acknowledge the segment is commercially real and not inherently wrong to serve
Identify the extra responsibility: young audiences are more susceptible to body image pressure, FOMO, and impulsive spending
Suggest concrete guardrails: honest imagery, avoiding aggressive urgency tactics, being mindful of parental context
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think it's wrong for a brand to serve that age group, they have real spending power and real style interests, but I do think the responsibility is higher than marketing to adults, because younger audiences are more affected by body image messaging and more likely to act on urgency tactics without weighing the consequences the way an adult might. I'd want any brand I worked for to be more careful there specifically, avoiding heavily retouched or unrealistic bodies in that messaging, and being cautious with high-pressure countdown or scarcity tactics aimed at that age group. It's a segment where I think 'is this technically legal' isn't a high enough bar, the question should be closer to whether I'd be comfortable with a younger sibling seeing it and being influenced by it.

commonMistakes: Refusing to engage with the segment as inherently exploitative
Treating young consumers identically to adult consumers with no extra care
No concrete guardrails proposed, only vague concern
followUps: Would you personally decline to work on a campaign that used urgency tactics aimed at that age group?

question: A creative director asks you to approve retouching that noticeably slims a model beyond what she actually looks like. What do you do?
lookingFor: Willingness to raise a genuine concern professionally rather than either silently complying or reacting purely emotionally.

bullets: Show they'd raise the concern rather than silently approving it
Frame the pushback constructively, referencing brand risk and honesty, not just personal discomfort
Show realistic awareness they may not have full authority to overrule the decision, and describe what they'd do next
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I wouldn't just approve it and move on, I'd raise it directly, probably by asking what the retouching is actually trying to fix, because often the honest answer is nothing functional, it's just chasing an unrealistic ideal that doesn't reflect the model or the brand's stated values. I'd frame the pushback practically as well as ethically, pointing out that audiences increasingly notice and call out obvious retouching, so it's a real brand risk, not just a personal objection. If I genuinely didn't have the authority to change the decision, I'd document my concern and raise it with whoever does, rather than quietly letting it go, because I'd want a record that I flagged it rather than just complying.

commonMistakes: Silently approving it to avoid conflict
Refusing outright with no attempt to raise it constructively through the right channel
Framing the objection purely as personal opinion with no practical brand argument
followUps: What would you do if the creative director dismissed your concern outright?

question: Imagine you have a fixed marketing budget for a new collection launch and have to split it between paid social ads, PR and press seeding, and an in-store event. How would you think about dividing it?
lookingFor: Structured reasoning about the different roles each channel plays rather than an arbitrary split.

bullets: Explain what each channel is actually good at: reach and conversion for ads, credibility and earned coverage for PR, emotional connection for events
Note the split should depend on the brand's stage and goal, not a fixed formula
Show they'd want some way to measure and reallocate mid-campaign rather than setting it once and leaving it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I wouldn't split it evenly, because each channel is doing a different job. Paid social is what actually drives volume and measurable conversion, PR and press seeding builds credibility and reach I can't easily buy, since a positive mention in a publication people trust carries weight an ad doesn't, and the event is really about depth, the small group of people who leave as genuine advocates. If this is a newer brand still building awareness, I'd weight more toward PR and paid reach; if it's an established brand launching to an existing loyal base, I'd probably lean more into the event and let paid social support it. I'd also want to build in a checkpoint partway through the launch to see what's actually converting and be willing to shift budget from a channel that's underperforming.

commonMistakes: Splitting the budget evenly with no reasoning
Describing only one channel in depth and dismissing the others
No mention of tracking or reallocating budget once the campaign is live
followUps: If early results showed the event drastically outperforming ads, what would you do?

question: A day before a major campaign launches, an investigative report breaks alleging poor labour conditions at one of the brand's supplier factories. As part of the marketing team, what would you want to happen?
lookingFor: Composed, structured crisis reasoning that doesn't default to denial or panic, and recognises marketing's limited but real role.

bullets: Recommend pausing or delaying the celebratory launch messaging rather than proceeding as if nothing happened
Note marketing's role is not to spin the allegations away, but to support an honest, fast internal investigation and communicate transparently once facts are known
Show awareness that a defensive or dismissive public response usually causes more damage than the original story
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My first instinct would be to pause the celebratory launch content, because pushing out cheerful campaign messaging while a serious labour allegation is breaking would look tone-deaf at best. I don't think marketing's job in that moment is to spin the story away, it's to support whoever's actually investigating the claim internally and make sure any public statement is honest about what's known and what isn't yet, rather than a defensive denial that could unravel later. I'd want us to be the team pushing for transparency rather than the team trying to bury the story, because a defensive non-answer tends to generate more coverage than a straightforward acknowledgment that the claim is being taken seriously. Getting the campaign timing right again would come after the more urgent problem was actually being addressed.

commonMistakes: Recommending the campaign proceed unchanged to avoid disruption
Suggesting marketing should try to spin or bury the story
No distinction between marketing's role and the investigation itself
followUps: What would you say if the allegations later turned out to be exaggerated by the report?

question: Why has it become harder for fashion brands to prove exactly which marketing channel is actually driving a sale?
lookingFor: A genuinely informed understanding of the attribution problem in modern marketing, not just a vague reference to 'tracking'.

bullets: Explain that a customer journey often crosses many touchpoints, an ad, a friend's post, a search, before purchase, making a single channel hard to credit
Mention privacy changes and cookie deprecation have removed some of the tracking that used to stitch that journey together
Note the practical consequence: brands rely more on modelled estimates, brand lift studies, or their own first-party signals than perfect tracking
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Part of it is that a real purchase journey is rarely one clean click, someone might see an ad, forget about it, then see a friend wearing the item, search the brand a week later, and finally buy through a completely different link, so crediting any single channel is already messy. What's made it harder recently is that privacy changes and the loss of third-party cookies have taken away a lot of the cross-site tracking that used to at least approximate that journey. In practice that means brands lean more on things like brand lift surveys, holdout tests where they deliberately withhold ads from a group to see the difference, and their own first-party data, rather than expecting a perfectly clean attribution number. I think it's made marketing measurement more honest in a way, because the old numbers were often more confident than the tracking really justified.

commonMistakes: Vaguely blaming 'tracking issues' with no explanation of the mechanism
Not mentioning multi-touchpoint journeys as part of the problem
No mention of how brands are adapting, like lift studies or first-party data
followUps: What's a holdout test, and how would you design one for a fashion campaign?

question: Extending a size range is expensive, more fabric, more grading, more inventory complexity. How would you make the case to a brand that it's still worth doing?
lookingFor: Ability to build a genuine business case for inclusivity that goes beyond a purely values-based appeal.

bullets: Acknowledge the real cost honestly rather than dismissing it as trivial
Build a commercial case: underserved market size, customer loyalty, reduced returns from better fit
Note the reputational risk of visibly excluding a large part of the population in current market conditions
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I wouldn't pretend the cost isn't real, extending a range genuinely adds complexity to grading, production, and stock planning, so I wouldn't try to argue it's free. The case I'd make is that a huge share of potential customers are currently being told, implicitly, that the brand isn't for them, and that's not a small missed market, it's often a majority-sized one depending on the category. I'd also point to fit as a returns issue, since a lot of returns happen because sizing didn't work, and getting sizing right for more bodies can actually reduce that cost elsewhere. And there's a reputational piece too, a visibly narrow size range increasingly reads as out of touch, so I'd frame it as closing a real gap in both revenue and brand perception, not just a values statement.

commonMistakes: Dismissing the cost concern instead of engaging with it honestly
Making a purely moral appeal with no commercial argument
Not connecting sizing to returns or fit-related cost
followUps: How would you research whether extending the range would actually pay off before committing to it?

question: Live commerce is enormous in China but has taken much longer to catch on in Western markets. Why do you think that gap exists?
lookingFor: Awareness of a real cross-market difference in consumer behaviour and infrastructure, with reasoning beyond a surface observation.

bullets: Mention infrastructure and habit: integrated super-apps and payment systems in China made the format frictionless earlier
Note different trust and entertainment habits: livestream shopping hosts function like trusted personalities in a way that took longer to establish in the West
Acknowledge the gap is closing, citing platforms pushing the format harder now
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A big part of it is infrastructure, platforms like Taobao and WeChat had shopping, payment, and social features integrated years before Western platforms caught up, so live commerce had a frictionless path to purchase almost from the start. There's also a trust and habit difference, live shopping hosts in China built up huge, almost celebrity-level trust as reliable product experts over years, and that kind of trusted-host culture is newer in Western markets, where influencer trust has traditionally been more about lifestyle content than direct product recommendation. I do think the gap is closing though, with platforms clearly pushing hard to replicate that model now that in-app checkout has caught up technically. I'd guess habit is now the bigger barrier left, more than the technology.

commonMistakes: Attributing the gap purely to 'cultural differences' with no specific mechanism
Ignoring the infrastructure and payment integration angle
Treating the gap as permanent rather than closing
followUps: What would it take for live commerce to become a default shopping habit in a Western market?

question: Buy now, pay later options at checkout have been shown to increase basket size, especially among younger shoppers who are more likely to overspend. Should a fashion brand keep promoting it heavily in its marketing?
lookingFor: Balanced ethical reasoning about a genuinely common, profitable feature that carries real financial risk for some customers.

bullets: Acknowledge the commercial reality: it's a legitimate, widely offered payment option that does increase conversion
Address the real risk honestly: it can encourage overspending, particularly among financially inexperienced younger shoppers
Propose a middle position, like offering it without aggressively pushing it in creative messaging
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think offering buy now, pay later is wrong in itself, it's a legitimate payment method that a lot of financially responsible people use deliberately, and removing it just because some people misuse it feels paternalistic. But I do think there's a difference between offering it quietly as an option and actively pushing it in ad creative as a way to make an item feel more affordable than it is, especially when a lot of the audience is young and building their first spending habits. My position would be to keep it available at checkout because customers should be able to choose it, but I'd be uncomfortable with marketing that uses it as the headline hook to encourage bigger baskets, particularly on channels skewing younger. I think there's a real line between offering a tool and leaning on it to drive impulse spending.

commonMistakes: Rejecting BNPL entirely with no acknowledgment of its legitimate use
Endorsing aggressive promotion with no reflection on the overspending risk
No distinction between offering it and actively pushing it in creative
followUps: Would your position change if internal data showed BNPL customers had a much higher return and default rate?

question: Fashion has swung between loud, logo-heavy branding and 'quiet luxury' with almost no visible branding at all. What does that swing tell you about how status signalling works?
lookingFor: Genuine trend analysis that connects a surface-level style shift to underlying consumer psychology, not just naming the trend.

bullets: Explain logomania as overt status signalling aimed at broad, immediate recognition
Explain quiet luxury as signalling to a narrower, more knowing audience through cut, fabric, or subtle detail rather than a visible logo
Connect the swing to a deeper idea: status signals shift when the original signal becomes too widely accessible or associated with the wrong audience
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Logomania works by making status instantly legible to almost anyone, a visible logo says 'expensive' to a stranger across the street. Quiet luxury flips that, it signals mainly to people who already know what an unlabelled cut or a specific fabric weight actually costs, so it's status aimed at a narrower, more informed audience rather than a broad one. I think the swing happens because once a loud logo becomes accessible through counterfeits or diffusion lines, it stops working as effectively for the original audience it was meant to signal to, so status has to move somewhere less easily copied. It's a good reminder that a lot of fashion marketing isn't really about the product, it's about maintaining a signal's exclusivity, and that signal keeps having to relocate.

commonMistakes: Naming both trends with no explanation of the underlying signalling logic
Treating it as pure aesthetics with no connection to status or accessibility
Assuming one trend is simply superior rather than explaining the cycle
followUps: Which trend do you think will dominate next, and what would trigger the next swing?

question: Why do so many fashion houses launch a fragrance or beauty line, and what's the marketing logic behind it beyond just extra revenue?
lookingFor: Understanding of brand extension and the halo effect as a strategic concept, not just a surface observation about diversification.

bullets: Explain the accessibility logic: a fragrance lets a much wider audience buy into the brand at a far lower price point than clothing
Explain the halo effect: owning even a small, affordable brand item builds emotional attachment that can pull the buyer toward the main line later
Note the risk: overextending or a poor-quality extension can dilute the core brand's prestige
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A big part of the logic is accessibility, most people will never buy a runway piece, but almost anyone can afford a fragrance, so it becomes the entry point where a much wider audience actually gets to own a piece of the brand. That matters beyond the immediate sale because of the halo effect, someone who buys and loves the fragrance builds a real emotional connection to the brand, and that connection can eventually pull them toward the clothing line once they can afford it, or at least keeps the brand present in their life between purchases. The risk is real too, if the fragrance or beauty line feels cheap or off-brand, it can quietly cheapen the perception of the whole house rather than reinforcing it, so the licensing and quality control decisions behind it matter just as much as the marketing. I find it a good example of how a brand extension is really a long-term relationship strategy disguised as a product launch.

commonMistakes: Explaining it only as 'extra revenue' with no deeper strategic reasoning
Not mentioning the halo effect or emotional entry-point logic
Ignoring the risk of dilution from a poorly executed extension
followUps: Can you think of a brand extension that you think damaged the core brand rather than strengthening it?
